title: how i built self learning trading bot with ai (no api costs)
author: Cool_Big2955
selftext:
hey guys, just wanted share my setup since see alot people ask about this. i run stock bot on alpaca + traderspost and crypto bot on binance but the ai part is different then most think.

execution is 100% deterministic hardcoded rules like anchor zones + atr trailing. no ai ever touch live orders or make decisions in real time. speed is first priority here.

the ai (qwen2.5:3b local via ollama) only runs in background AFTER trade close. it score if manual exit was better than auto stop historically and update weights slowly. never touch live orders at all.

for crypto bot same logic but more volatile so manual overrides get logged as high score events. bot learn which conditions need human review vs auto execution. still not fully autonomous and thats intentional.

why do it this way?

no api costs (local model free after download)

execution never wait for inference

learning happen offline safely

human oversight where volatility demand it

not claiming perfection or anything. just sharing what working for me with $102k stock portfolio + recent crypto tests. happy answer questions about logic if anyone curious.

current positions live right now:

AAPL: 31.0 shares @ $314.41 → Now $340.03 (+8.15%)

AMD: 40.0 shares @ $524.42 → Now $606.20 (+15.59%)

META: 15.0 shares @ $649.35 → Now $730.93 (+12.56%)

PLTR: 58.0 shares @ $171.83 → Now $184.35 (+7.29%)

DIS: 93.0 shares @ $107.39 → Now $104.86 (-2.36%)

if wanna try yourself just install ollama in cmd/terminal and run ollama pull qwen2.5:3b. takes like 2mins setup works great for trading logic without burning cash. add AI\_MODEL=qwen2.5:3b to your .env file.

not saying its better than claude its definitely not lol but if budget concern its worth testing. let me know if have questions! happy 2 help

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Logging crypto manual overrides as high-score events could teach qwen2.5:3b to favor intervention just because a human intervened. After a manual exit, do you keep a simulated position running with the original ATR trailing logic until its stop triggers? That would give you a paired outcome for scoring the override, including fees and the extra time exposed. Without that continuation, the manual exit has an observed result but the automatic exit you're comparing it with may not. I'd separate “human requested review” from “human exit improved the outcome” in the labels.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
keeping the model off the order path is the right call. most setups that blow up have inference sitting between the signal and the fill.

what I'd worry about is the weight updates. manual overrides are rare, so the model learns from a tiny sample, and each update gets judged on the same trades that produced it. a loop like that will always look like it's improving. cheap fix: freeze a copy of the weights each month, run it alongside the live one on paper, and only keep an update if the new weights beat the frozen copy on trades neither had seen yet.

also, those open positions are mostly riding a strong tape, so they can't tell you much about the exit logic either way. the exits worth learning from are the ones in a down week.

comments.author: koryuken
comments.body: It's an interesting experiment, but imo its the opposite of a good design imo. You don't want the system to learn off short term events, because it's learning off noise. This is why people backtest with longer horizons. What will likely happen is your bots will be like a squirrel chasing a nut, and always lagging behind.

comments.author: BlackVaultQuantNexus
comments.body:
The separation between deterministic execution and offline AI analysis is the part I find most useful here.



How are you preventing the post-trade label from becoming discretionary hindsight? Specifically:



\- What is the target variable for deciding that a manual exit was “better”?

\- Is there an untouched holdout period that weight updates never see?

\- How much can one closed trade change a weight?

\- What condition rolls the updated weights back if shadow performance degrades?

\- Does the model only produce structured labels, or can it directly modify numeric parameters?



Keeping the model outside live execution reduces one class of risk, but the learning loop can still overfit if its labels and update limits are not tightly defined.

replies.author: NefariousnessOpening
replies.body:
This could be a challenge to adapt to in terms of thinking, I will try to articulate clearly. The way I have been most successful is by using basically every model I can. Around 2k models form a collection or inventory of available models in my gateway. Some are just duplicate models that are available at multiple providers. The model and provider list auto updates in two ways. The providers update frequently and typical have an endpoint on their api to query the current model list. The other way is by performance and relevance. Models that are fit for commonly tasks are selected more often. Models selected that then perform well are given a higher rating. Models and even providers can end up ranking down over time and being ejected from the list but there’s also so many new models and providers coming out with (free quotas), the size ends up staying the same or often just slowly increasing. Some local models I have also been using are now specifically selected per project and most likely fine tuned for the project. Qwen3.x 0.6B - 3B, Gemma4 (smaller 2-4B), LFM2.5 2.6B, ibm granite 4 nano, SmolVLM, Needle 3, prism ML 1bit, miniCPM5… those are some I have found working well by use case and with the right tools, fine tuning, system design around it, etc 

The model is not irrelevant but the harness matters more, the bigger picture system designed around the model(s) and harness matters most. Using many different models both local, small, cloud, open source and frontier all as one system is the only way I can see myself implementing AI/LLMs at this point

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: This split is smart keeping the local model completely out of the live execution path (deterministic ATR/anchor rules) and only using it for offline scoring after the fact avoids the two biggest failure modes people run into: inference latency stalling an order, and a model second-guessing a fill mid-trade. Curious how you're weighting the historical exit score though is it purely comparing manual exit price vs where auto-stop would've triggered, or does it also factor in how much longer you held past the stop before manually closing? That timing piece seems like it'd matter a lot for whether the 'high score' events actually generalize to future similar setups vs just being hindsight-biased on this particular run: [claude.ai](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.author: Cool_Big2955
replies.body:
yeah good point about the timing  honestly its mostly price based right now but i do track duration in the learning log.

the score compares manual exit price vs where auto-stop wouldve triggered BUT if i held way past the stop (like days) without much extra gain it gets a lower weight than a quick 30min hold with same profit. dont want bot to learn that "waiting forever is always better" just because one lucky trade worked out.

still tweaking this part tho. sometimes hard to quantify opportunity cost of capital binding vs raw dollar difference. open to suggestions if you have ideas on weighting time decay!

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
For weighting opportunity cost, one approach that tends to work better than raw duration penalties: normalize the exit score by return-per-unit-time rather than penalizing duration directly, something like (profit captured) / (hours held), so a 30-min hold and a 3-day hold with the same dollar profit get properly differentiated without hand-tuning a decay curve. To actually capture capital-binding cost rather than just time, you could also compare the realized return against what your bot's average trade return-per-hour was across that same holding window, if a position sat flat for 2 days while your average setup would've cycled through 4 other trades in that time, that's real opportunity cost even if the eventual exit price looks fine in isolation. Worth logging both numbers separately (raw price-based score and time-normalized score) rather than collapsing into one metric early, since you'll want to inspect cases where they disagree, that's usually where the interesting signal is about whether 'waiting it out' is a real edge or just variance.

If event-driven catalysts ever factor into your exit logic (news, earnings, macro prints causing the extended holds), EventTrader's event data might be worth plugging into that scoring layer too. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)
